newsitem.title: USA: Blood protein found to shrink cancer tumors.
newsitem.headline: Blood protein found to shrink cancer tumors.

text.p: A naturally produced protein in the blood has been found to shrink cancerous tumors and may prove to be a powerful weapon in stopping the disease from developing into a terminal illness, according to a study in Friday's edition of the medical journal Cell.

Researchers at Children's Hospital in Boston reported the discovery of a potent inhibitor of new blood cells, vital in the growth of tumors. Cells in cancerous tumors produce proteins that stimulate the growth of new blood vessels, which feed tumors with oxygen, growth factors and proteins and also proteins that inhibit blood vessel growth.

Dr. Michael O'Reilly, a research fellow at the department of surgery at Children's Hospital, discovered a new inhibitor, called endostatin, which he believes is the most potent of a number of inhibitors discovered to date.

The researchers found in a 30-day study that a variety of tumors in mice treated with endostatin shrunk to microscopic dormant lesions, Dr. Judah Folkman, who led the research team, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"If they work in patients as well as they work in laboratories, and that's a big if, then one might hope that they improve our ability to treat cancer by adding them to current therapy," Folkman said.
Traditional cancer therapies often cause severe side effects because they slow cell division, particularly in the gut and bond marrow where cells divide rapidly.

But endostatin and another inhibitor called angiostatin, discovered by O'Reilly a few years ago, were found to slow cell growth only in blood vessels and the heart, where cells divide much less frequently.

While some cancer therapies may develop a resistance to further treatment, endostatin and angiostatin do not appear to cause a buildup of drug resistance, indicating they could be used whenever needed, Folkman said.
"If you stop (the treatments), the tumor will come back, but if you keep treating the mice, they are very healthy. They did not have side effects," he said.

Inhibitors also have been found to supress the growth of metastasis, the transfer of tumor cells to another site in the body. In purified forms, other inhibitors have halted growth of cancerous tumors in animal and human clinical trials. At least nine of such substances are currently in trials.

EntreMed Inc., a Rockville, Maryland-based biopharmaceutical company, has worldwide rights to endostatin and other inhibitors and is pursuing pre-clinical trials on angiostatin with its partner, Bristol-Myers Squibb Co.
Angiostatin was the first inhibitor found that caused human tumors growing in mice to shrink. Similiar tests for endostatin will be conducted this year, Folkman said.
